prompt.context: Our client is a major global shoe manufacturer. They are currently #2 in the US and are seeking to dethrone the #1 shoe manufacturer. They have tried several strategies in the past and none have worked. They are now looking to purchase the #3 shoe manufacturer to see if combined, they can overcome #1. Manufacturer #3 has quoted a price of $480M preliminarily for the sale.
prompt.question: Should our client (the #2 shoe manufacturer) go forward with the acquisition of the #3 shoe manufacturer at $480M?

clarifying_info.q: Do both manufacturers make similar products?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, both make similar shoes, primarily dress shoes.

clarifying_info.q: Do they sell through the same channels?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, both sell in roughly the same places.

clarifying_info.q: How is #3's product quality perceived relative to #2?
clarifying_info.a: The #3 manufacturer's shoes are perceived as being of lower quality.

clarifying_info.q: Would the two brands remain separate after acquisition?
clarifying_info.a: Despite being one company, the two brands could remain separate; however they would not want to market against each other in advertising as they have been doing.
Yes, there is a risk of market cannibalization, which could lead to total sales being lower.

clarifying_info.q: Could the combined ownership affect consumer perceptions?
clarifying_info.a: If the brands were seen as being produced together, it could affect consumer perceptions and also affect sales.
Yes, there is a possibility for synergies leading to more efficient operations and improved profit margins for both companies.

framework: Target attractiveness: quality perception, market position, product/channel overlap
Economics of the deal / valuation: payback period analysis, NPV of cash flows, comparable multiples, book value
Fit with acquirer: synergies (revenue and cost), cannibalization risk, brand dilution risk
Alternatives to acquisition: organic growth, other targets, partnerships

questions.prompt: Phase 1 — Valuation: What would you take into account when valuing this deal, and what is a fair price to pay for #3?
questions.guidance: Candidate should mention multiples/comparables, NPV/cash flow analysis, and book value. Then execute the aggregate cash flow / payback analysis using the provided data: #2 revenues $1B at 10% margin = $100M profit/yr; #3 revenues $750M at 8% margin = $60M profit/yr; 8-year payback period. Fair price = #3 profit x payback = $480M. Candidate should note this exactly matches the quoted price, meaning at current performance levels the deal just breaks even on the payback criterion — and should flag that synergies or margin deterioration could shift this significantly.

math.setup: Payback price = annual profit of target x payback period years
steps: Coincides exactly with the quoted $480M price
math.answer: $480M — deal is fairly priced at current margins with an 8-year payback

questions.prompt: Phase 2 — Synergies: If the deal increases #2's total profit by 15% and #3's profit by $10M/yr, what is the maximum price #2 should be willing to pay?
questions.guidance: Candidate must compute the combined incremental annual profit from synergies, then multiply by the payback period to derive a maximum willingness-to-pay. Should compare to the $480M quoted price and conclude the deal is attractive. Should also discuss types of synergies: revenue synergies (volume pricing, retailer negotiation leverage) and cost synergies (materials consolidation, plant consolidation, distribution network combination).

math.setup: Incremental annual profit from synergies = (#2 profit x 15% uplift) + (#3 incremental profit $10M)
steps: Total incremental annual profit = $15M + $70M = $85M (note: this is total profit from #3 plus #2 uplift, not purely incremental over baseline; the implied max price uses all profit flowing through the deal)
Alternatively: max price = incremental gain from deal x 8 years = $85M x 8 = $680M
math.answer: Maximum willingness-to-pay = $680M; quoted $480M is well below this, making the deal attractive if synergy assumptions hold

questions.prompt: Phase 2 — Plant consolidation: The client has 3 US plants and the target has 3. How would you decide how many to shut down?
questions.guidance: Candidate should discuss: existing capacity utilisation of each plant; economics/profitability of each plant; strategic rationale (proximity to raw material inputs and distribution outputs); cultural and political considerations for the combined company; marginal cost of production per plant (prefer lower); and the option to outsource production to third-party plants rather than retaining any of the six.

questions.prompt: Phase 3 — Risks: What are the key risks of the acquisition and how would you mitigate them?
questions.guidance: Core risks are cannibalization (both brands sell similar dress shoes through the same channels) and brand dilution / consumer perception damage (if customers learn #3's lower-quality brand is now owned by the same parent). Mitigation approaches include: running focus groups to assess consumer reactions to co-ownership; broader customer surveys; tracking sales and customer demographic shifts post-merger; maintaining strict brand separation; careful communication strategy to avoid linking the two brands publicly.

brainstorming.prompt: What types of synergies could #2 realistically hope to realize from this acquisition?

categories.name: Revenue synergies
ideas: Volume-based pricing leverage with large retail partners
Combined distribution network increases shelf presence for both brands
Stronger negotiating position with department stores and footwear chains

categories.name: Cost synergies — Materials
ideas: Consolidate purchasing of raw materials (leather, rubber, etc.) to negotiate lower unit prices
Reduce supplier base and achieve scale economies

categories.name: Cost synergies — Manufacturing
ideas: Consolidate the six US plants into fewer, higher-utilisation facilities
Shut down highest-cost or lowest-utilisation plants
Share best-practice manufacturing processes across the combined entity
Explore outsourcing to lower-cost third-party manufacturers

categories.name: Cost synergies — Distribution & Logistics
ideas: Optimise logistics routes across a larger volume base

categories.name: Cost synergies — G&A / Overhead
ideas: Eliminate duplicate corporate functions (finance, HR, legal, IT)
Consolidate marketing spend; cease head-to-head advertising between the two brands

recommendation: Our client should proceed with the acquisition at the $480M quoted price

At current profit levels the deal exactly meets the 8-year payback requirement; with realistic synergies (15% uplift for #2 and $10M/yr for #3) the implied fair value rises to $680M, meaning $480M represents a significant discount to intrinsic value
risks: Synergy assumptions may not materialise — particularly cost synergies from plant consolidation require rigorous due diligence
Cannibalization: both brands sell similar products through the same channels, which could erode combined revenues
Brand dilution: consumers may downgrade their perception of #2's brand if association with the lower-quality #3 brand becomes public
Integration execution risk: restructuring costs, employee turnover, and operational disruption could temporarily reduce margins below baseline
next_steps: Commission customer research (focus groups and surveys) to quantify cannibalization and brand-perception risk before closing
Conduct detailed plant-by-plant capacity and cost analysis to validate plant-consolidation synergy assumptions
Engage independent financial advisors to verify #3's revenue and margin figures through due diligence
Develop a brand-separation communication strategy to mitigate consumer perception risk post-close
